uniequip_002_liesel:
The baton passes over the last note of the score on the brass plate before her, and the performance ends amid unbroken applause. Liesel turns to bow to the audience as she always does, and as her gaze sweeps the hall she catches something inexplicably out of place. It is a Caprinae woman of about Paula's age, a trace of unease hidden in her eyes and, together with it, a kind of suppressed joy—as though she were listening to some melody long since gone, one only she can hear.
Why should a piece so bright and lively bring on feelings like these? It was Mama Paula's favorite. Liesel had pestered her for months to work out every detail of those modes, because she was intoxicated by the abandon and the freedom in them, unfettered as a dancer on a boundless plain. Mama Paula had also told her not to fixate on accuracy, but to imagine the weightless sensation of being flung up into the clouds...
'Thank you. I thought... I thought I would never hear a piece like that again.
'I heard a melody like it on a street corner back home. It was the freest sound I have ever heard. But the guards drove that old wandering musician away afterward...
'The spire musicians said that music like that was wayward and out of time, a desecration of the highest art. That only musicians with no formal training would ever call such a thing... beautiful.
'But is beauty really something that anyone gets to define...?'
The woman falls silent for a long while. In that place Liesel has never set foot in, there seems to lie some pain that cannot be spoken aloud—perhaps one of the reasons Mama Paula came to Nuova Volsinii all those years ago. Liesel remembers what Mama Paula once wrote beside a score she had copied out by hand:
Expression and taste have never been anyone's privilege, and love cannot be barred. There is no need to fear censure or scrutiny. So long as one is willing to pour oneself out freely, people can meet one another as equals; those loves will bring about solidarity, and people will come together because of them, and something new will take shape.
Back then Liesel had not really understood; she only felt the words were beautiful and warm, just like Mama Paula herself. Now, facing the longing and the sorrow in this woman's eyes, she suddenly understands: this piece that Mama Paula loved best also carried the conviction on which she founded the orchestra. Not because the music was beautiful enough, but because it was the voice inside musicians who love music—and once you have taken up an instrument, that voice deserves to be heard.
She has come one step closer to Mama Paula.
'My mother left Leithanien and brought this piece here with her, and she taught it to me. Since it has come to a place where people are able to hear it, the orchestra will make it worth hearing as well.'
Liesel holds out her hand.
'Welcome to Nuova Volsinii. At our next performance, we will play it again.'
The woman before her smiles—a very light smile, as though some confusion had dissolved into nothing.
'Thank you... I will come.'
Liesel watches the woman go, and thinks of Mama Paula standing on the podium, and of that small line written on the score—
Dedicated to all musicians.
Liesel Meminger draws a deep breath and lifts her head.
Tomorrow there is tomorrow's performance to prepare for.
